newsitem.title: USA: No immediate plans to use EEP yet - USDA official.
newsitem.headline: No immediate plans to use EEP yet - USDA official.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department does not have any immediate plans to restart its grain subsidy program, but will do so if European subsidies begin to hurt U.S. grain sales, the Agriculture Department General Sales Manager told Reuters Monday.

"If we see that this (European subsidies) really begins to affect our ability to market our crop, we will have to react at some point, but it's not planned for the immediate future," said Chris Goldthwait.

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman had said earlier on Monday that European subsidies cannot "go on forever" before the United States re-activates its Export Enhancement Program to keep U.S. farmers competitive.
Goldthwait noted, however, that "too much" should not be read into Glickman's comments, and indicated that as long as U.S. grain sales continue to be steady, Washington will refrain from using EEP.
But Goldthwait said that the European subsidies are a concern, because they have been at higher levels than in the past. "We don't see why the subsidies need to be so large."
Goldthwait said the department will be ready to move, if the decision is made to restart EEP.
"If we got into a situation where we thought it was really necesary to restart the program, I think we would know what to do. We would have a good idea of what markets to look at," he said.
Goldthwait also said that at discussions last week with Russian officials, the head of Russia's largest grain buying company expressed interest in buying U.S. wheat and/or wheat flour.

Goldthwait said that financing of future grain purchases was discussed, and that U.S. officials told the Russian that Washington would consider increasing Russia's GSM-102 credit allocations once a remaining $25 million allocation is utilized.

The USDA official also noted that in response to inquiries from Russian officials, U.S. officials said that if the agency restarts the EEP, Russia would likely be on the list of recipient countries, as it has been in the past.
Goldthwait said he will be meeting with Russian officials again to discuss purchases, but said nothing has been scheduled yet.
He said no levels of purchases were specifically discussed, but speculated that there could be modest purchases in the very immediate future.

"The impression I got was that a lot of this would be for the Russian far east, so I would expect there to be some level of purchases periodically -- pretty much anytime," Goldthwait said. "We're not talking gigantic purchases, but there could be some small purchases anyway."
